keyVerseText: And the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ἐπιγράφω (epigráphō) is formed from the preposition ἐπί (epi), meaning 'upon' or 'over,' and the verb γράφω (graphō), meaning 'to write.' Thus, its root meaning is to write upon or inscribe over a surface. This literal sense of marking something 'on top of' or 'over' a base adds a physical or visible dimension to the act of writing, emphasizing the idea of an inscription that is meant to be seen and recognized, rather than just written in a general sense.
usageInScripture: The word ἐπιγράφω appears five times in the New Testament, where it is translated variously as 'written over,' 'inscription,' 'write,' 'will I write,' and 'written thereon.' This range of translations reflects the word’s core idea of writing or inscribing something on a surface, often with a public or formal intent. Its consistent use in contexts involving inscriptions or titles, such as the superscription on Jesus' cross, highlights its specialized meaning of marking or engraving words visibly and deliberately.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἐπιγράφω enriches our grasp of how God’s truth and revelation are communicated and made manifest. Just as an inscription is meant to be permanent and publicly displayed, the truths of Scripture and the identity of Christ are ‘written upon’ the hearts of believers and visibly proclaimed in the world. This word reminds us that God’s message is not hidden but boldly inscribed for all to see, calling us to recognize and own the divine inscription of Christ as King and Savior. It also points to the spiritual reality that God’s covenant and promises are etched into the believer’s life, signifying a lasting and authoritative claim.
keyVerseReflection: In Mark 15:26, the phrase 'the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS' uses ἐπιγράφω to describe the official inscription placed above Jesus on the cross. This word emphasizes that the title was not just written but prominently inscribed for public display, marking Jesus’ identity and the charge against Him in a visible, undeniable way. It underscores the irony and profound truth that Jesus is indeed the King, a title inscribed in suffering yet ultimately vindicated.
